title: HOI AN BAI CHOI: A CULTURAL SOUL IN THE HEART OF THE ANCIENT TOWN
author: Tường Vy
summary: Amidst the rhythmic flow of modern life, Hoi An preserves an enchanting stillness where heritage doesn't sit behind glass, but lives through every beat of the clapper and every rustic chant. Far more ...
content_html:
Amidst the rhythmic flow of modern life, Hoi An preserves an enchanting stillness where heritage doesn't sit behind glass, but lives through every beat of the clapper and every rustic chant. Far more than a folk game, Bai Choi has become the breath and soul of the town - an invisible thread connecting past to present, weaving a tapestry of warmth in the heart of the moss-covered Ancient Town.

Amidst the silent golden walls draped in moss and century-old wooden houses, Hoi An invites travelers not only through its visual splendor but also through echoes from the past. These are the rhythmic beats of the wooden tocsin, the piercing melodies of the dan nhi (two-string fiddle), and the witty chants of the Bai Choi performers. For generations, this folk art has served as the soul and an inseparable cultural practice of the people of Hoi An.

Unlike many academic art forms, Hoi An’s Bai Choi originated from the breath of laboring life. In the old days, when farmers built huts (choi) on stilts to guard their crops, they created a way of singing back and forth between huts to stave off loneliness. Over time, those chants were refined and combined with a set of bamboo cards (bai) and unique performance styles to become a popular folk game. In 2017, the Art of Bai Choi in Central Vietnam was officially inscribed by UNESCO as an Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity, reaffirming its enduring value in the flow of the modern era.

The most unique aspect of Bai Choi lies in the seamless blend of music, poetry, and acting. At the center of the game are the Anh Hieu and Chi Hiệu (the male and female hosts) - versatile artists with a flair for improvisation. They do not merely draw cards and call out names; they weave in folk verses, proverbs, or self-composed rhythmic chants. The content of these songs is deeply humanistic, ranging from praising the love for the homeland and family piety to gentle satires of social vices. All are delivered in the characteristic Quang Nam accent, which is as rustic and sincere as the souls of the local people.

At the playground along the Hoai River, each round is a reunion between the past and the present. Players sit in elevated bamboo huts, holding their cards, listening intently to every lyric, and waiting in suspense for the beat of the tocsin to signal a win. This atmosphere attracts not only elders seeking to rediscover old memories but also foreign tourists who find themselves drawn to the vibrant, friendly energy. Here, the boundary between performer and spectator vanishes, replaced by bursts of laughter at a host’s graceful joke or applause when a lucky card is called.

In the context of rapid urbanization, Hoi An’s Bai Choi maintains a vigorous vitality thanks to the community's enthusiastic preservation. It is not confined to museums or traditional festivals but winds its way into every night in the ancient town, becoming a part of daily life. Sustaining Bai Choi is not just about keeping a game alive; it is about preserving a treasure trove of oral folk literature and the affectionate, meaningful lifestyle of Central Vietnamese people.

Visiting Hoi An as sunset falls and lanterns begin to glow, stopping by a bamboo hut to hear a chant is the best way to touch the spirit of the heritage. Bai Choi is more than just a beautiful cultural practice; it is an invisible thread connecting people to their roots, serving as a testament to a Hoi An that always knows how to renew itself based on solid traditional values.

title: MASKS BEHIND THE FAN: SATIRE AND MORALITY IN THE “VẠN” CARDS OF BAI CHOI
author: Tường Vy
summary: Behind every palm-leaf fan lies a story of hidden faces and social satire. In the world of Bai Choi, the Vạn (Myriad) suit serves as a vivid theatrical mirror, mocking the hypocrisies of the elite and...
content_html:
Behind every palm-leaf fan lies a story of hidden faces and social satire. In the world of Bai Choi, the Vạn (Myriad) suit serves as a vivid theatrical mirror, mocking the hypocrisies of the elite and the sharp tongues of the gossips. From the vulgar curls of Tam Quăn to the cunning 'failed monk' of Cửu Thầy, these cards are more than just pieces of wood - they are a humorous yet profound lesson in morality, teaching us to look past the masks people wear.

In the world of Bai Choi, the deck is more than a game - it is a gallery of social archetypes. While some cards celebrate fertility and nature, the Vạn (Myriad) suit offers a sharper, more satirical look at human nature. Symbolized by the recurring image of an official hiding behind a palm-leaf fan, this suit serves as a classic metaphor for hypocrisy: the "white-turned-black" mask used by those who conceal their true faces from the world.

Among this suit, three cards stand out for their vivid imagery and the biting wit they inspire in the performers: Tam Quăn, Thất Nhọn, and Cửu Thầy.

Tam Quăn: The "Curly" official

The name Tam Quăn literally means "Curly," and the card portrays a portly, vulgar official characterized by his distinctive curled beard. However, in the lively atmosphere of a Bai Choi performance, the Anh Hieu (male host) often plays with language. Due to local dialects, "Quăn" (curly) is frequently interchanged with "Quăng" (to throw).

The verses for this card often tell stories of startled lovers or hasty retreats, such as: "I was writing scrolls inside the communal hall / Hearing your husband's voice, I startled and threw down (quăng) my inkstone." Through this card, the audience is reminded that even the most "portly" officials are often caught in moments of undignified chaos.

Thất Nhọn: The Sharp-Tongued Schemer

If Tam Quăn represents vulgarity, Thất Nhọn (The Sharp One) represents deceit. The card features an elongated face with a pointed snout and slanted eyes - the quintessential look of a silver-tongued schemer. The "sharpness" refers to a pointed mouth, symbolizing the narrow-minded gossips and sycophants who plagued old administrative courts.

When this card is drawn, the performers engage in theatrical banter to satirize meddlers. A Chi Hieu might tease a man for his drinking debts, only for the Anh Hieu to retort: "And you’re no better, a wandering gossip; with a mouth so sharp (nhọn), you nag your husband like popping corn!" It is a playful yet pointed critique of those who use their words to wound others.

Cửu Thầy: The Failed Monk

Perhaps the most complex card in the Vạn suit is Cửu Thầy (also known as Cửu Chùa). This card depicts a "failed monk" who has donned the kasaya robe and the Five-Buddha hat but has failed to attain true enlightenment. His face, partially hidden behind the signature fan of the Vạn suit, still betrays a cunning and devious spirit.

Interestingly, despite the card’s satirical imagery, the verses called for Cửu Thầy often pivot toward a more humanistic message. Because the word "Thầy" (Master/Teacher) is a homonym for many respected figures, the performers use it to honor parents and educators: "In the future, when you repay your debts of gratitude / Never forget your parents’ labor or your teacher’s (thầy) grace."

The Mirror of the Fan

The charm of the Tam Quăn, Thất Nhọn, and Cửu Thầy cards lies in this duality. They use the stylized forms of dishonest mandarins and flawed characters to teach moral lessons. By mocking the "sharp mouths" and the "hidden faces" behind the fans, Bai Choi encourages its audience to live with transparency and gratitude.

The Art of Wordplay: The Chameleonic Spirit of the Chant

What truly breathes life into these cards is the remarkable linguistic flexibility of the Anh Hieu and Chit Hieu. In Bai Choi, the meaning of a card is never static; it is a living, breathing entity that shifts based on the performer’s wit and the audience's energy. Rather than being bound to the literal or historical definition of the card’s name, the performers utilize the rich tonal landscape of the Vietnamese language, particularly the Central dialect.

Through the clever use of homophones (words that sound the same) and near-synonyms, a card like Tam Quăn (Curly) can seamlessly transform into a story about Quăng (throwing), while Cửu Thầy (The Monk) becomes a poignant tribute to Thầy cô (teachers). This improvisational freedom allows the performers to bridge the gap between ancient satire and modern life, ensuring that the "soul" of the card is always relevant, humorous, and deeply resonant with the listeners' hearts.

title: A BRIEF LOOK INTO THE ORIGINS OF THE ART OF BAI CHOI
author: Báo Bình Định
summary: While the people of Kinh Bac are passionate about Quan Ho folk songs, those in Phu Tho cherish Xoan singing, and Southerners take pride in Don Ca Tai Tu, the people of Central Vietnam have now seen th...
content_html:
While the people of Kinh Bac are passionate about Quan Ho folk songs, those in Phu Tho cherish Xoan singing, and Southerners take pride in Don Ca Tai Tu, the people of Central Vietnam have now seen their wishes fulfilled as the art of Bai Choi singing has officially become a World Heritage.While the people of Kinh Bac are passionate about Quan Ho folk songs, those in Phu Tho cherish Xoan singing, and Southerners take pride in Don Ca Tai Tu, the people of Central Vietnam have now seen their wishes fulfilled as the art of Bai Choi singing has officially become a World Heritage.

On December 7, 2017, the 12th session of the UNESCO Intergovernmental Committee for the Safeguarding of the Intangible Cultural Heritage, held in Jeju, South Korea, inscribed the "Art of Bai Choi in Central Vietnam" on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.

While Bai Choi is a shared heritage across nine central provinces (from Quang Binh to Binh Thuan), Binh Dinh is widely regarded as its cradle.

From Forest Watchtowers to Folk Art

According to folklore researchers, Bai Choi originated in its primitive form as a card game (known as ho bai choi). It evolved into a close-knit and unique folk art reflecting the thoughts, emotions, and daily lives of people along the Central Coast.

Professor Hoang Chuong, Director General of the Center for Preservation and Promotion of National Culture, notes that while no written records exist, legends and artisans' oral histories trace its birth back to the late 16th and early 17th centuries. During this era, wild animals frequently raided crops and disturbed villagers. To protect their livelihoods, locals built high bamboo huts (choi) at the edge of the forest.

Young men were stationed in these huts to keep watch. If a wild beast appeared, they would beat drums and shout (ho) loudly to drive them away. To pass the time and combat loneliness during these long vigils, the guards began to communicate by singing and chanting back and forth between the huts.

Eventually, they developed a card game (similar to the Tu Sac or Tam Cuc games in the North) to play while singing. This combination of card gaming and chanting between huts became known as ho bai choi, the precursor to the art form we know today.

The Evolution into a Cultural Festival

Over time, these casual pastimes grew into organized festivals (Hoi Bai Choi). Some researchers also credit Dao Duy Tu (1572-1634) with its creation. After moving south to serve the Nguyen Lords, his first stop was Binh Dinh. Inspired by the mountain watchtowers, he reportedly adapted the concept into a card game played on huts, which eventually became a staple of Lunar New Year celebrations (Hoi Bai Choi Xuan).

Bai Choi is essentially "card playing on huts," but it is not just an open-air game. It is deeply intertwined with the art of performance led by the "Anh Hieu" (the master of ceremonies or host).

Gradually, winning or losing became secondary to the cultural experience. People attended these festivals primarily to hear the performers chant folk verses, proverbs, or witty improvisations. To meet the growing demand, performers began incorporating dramatic plots and stories into the singing.

Golden Age and Modern Revival

Between 1930 and 1940, to attract more viewers, artisans expanded from a single chant into four basic melodies: Xuan Nu, Co Ban, Xang Xe, and Ho Quang. Later, elements of Hat Boi (Classical Opera) were borrowed to enrich the repertoire.

The period of the resistance against the French (1945-1954) is considered the "golden age" of Bai Choi. Recognizing its immense popularity, the Party used the art form as a medium for propaganda. Soldiers and civilians alike sang Bai Choi everywhere, leading to a surge of new compositions rooted in daily life.

In 2000, Meritorious Artist Phan Ngan (Binh Dinh Bai Choi Opera Troupe) played a pivotal role in restoring the traditional spring festivals, recovering the card decks, and training a new generation of Anh Hieu performers. Today, the Art of Bai Choi is recognized as a National Intangible Cultural Heritage (2014) and a UNESCO Representative Heritage (2017). In Binh Dinh, it is no longer just a New Year's activity but a "specialty" of local folk culture, proudly shared with tourists from around the world.

title: BẠCH HUÊ AND NỌC ĐƯỢNG: THE SACRED HARMONY OF YIN AND YANG IN BAI CHOI CULTURE
author: Tường Vy
summary: In the rustic deck of Bai Choi, among the kings and commoners, there exist two cards that capture the rawest, most humanistic essence of Vietnamese folklore. Bach Hue and Noc Duong are not merely play...
content_html:
In the rustic deck of Bai Choi, among the kings and commoners, there exist two cards that capture the rawest, most humanistic essence of Vietnamese folklore. Bach Hue and Noc Duong are not merely playing pieces; they are vibrant symbols of the "fertility culture" (phồn thực) - a testament to the open-minded and harmonious spirit of the Central Vietnamese people.

The Art of Symbols: Yoni and Linga

At first glance, the imagery on these cards reveals a profound connection to ancient philosophies. The Bach Hue card (also affectionately called Bach Tuyet) features two inward-curving seaweed branches. This delicate design is a stylized representation of the Yoni, symbolizing the feminine, or Yin, energy of humanity.

In perfect contrast, the Noc Duong card (known in some regions as Noc Thuoc) showcases a stylized bird influenced by the bold art of the Central Highlands. This represents the Linga—the masculine, or Yang, energy. Together, they form the primal duality of existence.

Modern interpretations, such as the interlocking keychain designs, emphasize this physical connection. Like a complete puzzle, these two cards are natural counterparts, symbolizing the ultimate harmony and the cycle of life that sustains mankind.

The Wit of the Performers: Turning Desire into Art

What makes Bach Hue and Noc Duong truly come alive is the performance of the Anh Hieu and Chit Hieu. When these cards are drawn, the atmosphere shifts from casual play to a space of witty, subtle, and sophisticated storytelling.

The performers use poetic metaphors to address primal human desires with a deep sense of respect and humanism. For the Noc Duong card, they might chant with a mischievous wink: "A man possesses the wedge A woman blooms with nectar and a vessel to hold... A man guards the treasure, braced by the balls on both sides."

When Bach Hue appears, the chanting reminds the audience of the irresistible power of the feminine: "Even heroes cannot pass the Gate of Beauty... From commoners to Kings, it leaves everyone lingering and enamored it spares no one at all."

A Humanistic Legacy

In many cultures, topics of fertility and desire are often hushed or hidden. However, in the world of Bai Choi, they are celebrated as the "law of nature." Through the images of the seaweed and the bird, and the humorous verses of the artists, these cards bridge the gap between the sacred and the mundane. Bach Hue and Noc Duong serve as a reminder that Bai Choi is more than just entertainment; it is a cultural mirror reflecting the Vietnamese people’s liberated view of life, love, and the eternal balance of the universe.
